opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that inference at scale isn't a chip problem anymore, it's a systems problem.

When we started d-Matrix, a lot of the focus was rightly on the silicon. We built Corsair around digital in-memory compute because we saw that memory bandwidth, not raw compute, was the real bottleneck for generative inference. But as models grew, and especially as reasoning models and agentic workloads started generating far more tokens per query, it became clear that no single accelerator card serves a frontier model on its own. You're spreading the model across many devices, and the moment you do that, the interconnect, the networking, the power delivery, the cooling, and the software that orchestrates it all matter as much as the chip.

So if we just handed customers a PCIe card and said, "Good luck," we'd be leaving them to solve the hardest part themselves. Hyperscalers and neoclouds don't buy chips; they buy tokens per second per dollar, and tokens per watt, at the rack and data center level. To deliver on that, you have to think about how cards talk to each other within a server, how servers scale out across a rack, how you keep latency low when a model is sharded across dozens of devices, and how you fit within the power envelope a data center actually has.

That's why we've invested in rack-scale engineering, things like our scale-up and scale-out networking work and reference rack designs with partners. It lets us show customers a complete, deployable system with predictable performance, rather than a component they have to integrate and validate over many months. Time to deployment is a huge competitive factor right now. If a customer can roll in a rack and start serving low-latency inference quickly, that's what wins.

And frankly, it's also what the incumbents do. NVIDIA doesn't just sell GPUs anymore; they sell full racks. If you want to compete credibly in inference, you need to meet customers at that same level of integration, while offering better efficiency and lower latency. That's the bet we're making.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think a lot of people in the chip world underestimate. When we started d-Matrix, the easy assumption was that we're a silicon company, so our job ends at the chip. You tape it out, you put it on a card, you hand it to a customer. And that's just not how inference gets deployed anymore.

The reality is that nobody buys a chip. They buy a rack. The unit of deployment for a hyperscaler or a large enterprise is the rack, and increasingly it's a row of racks. So if you want your silicon to actually show up in production, you have to think about everything that sits between the die and the data center floor. How do these cards talk to each other? What does the interconnect look like? How do you handle power delivery and cooling at density? How does the software see the whole thing as one coherent pool of compute and memory instead of a bunch of individual accelerators?

For us specifically, because we built Corsair around in-memory compute and a chiplet architecture, the real payoff only shows up when you scale out. The whole point is that you keep the model weights close to the compute and you avoid constantly shuttling data back and forth. If you do that well on a single card but then bottleneck at the rack level, you've thrown away most of the advantage. So the interconnect and the topology aren't an afterthought for us. They're part of the product.

The other piece is that the customers we're talking to don't have time to be systems integrators. They want something they can slot into an existing data center with a known power envelope and a known thermal profile, and they want it to work with their orchestration stack on day one. If I show up with a great chip and no rack story, I'm asking them to do a lot of engineering on my behalf, and that's a very hard sell against the incumbents who already have that figured out.

So we deliberately went and hired people who had spent their careers building systems, not just silicon. People who'd done racks at the hyperscalers, people who understood the networking side, people who'd lived through the pain of deploying hardware at scale. It's a different muscle from chip design, and you can't fake it. Honestly, it's probably been one of the more important decisions we made, because it changed the conversation with customers from "interesting technology" to "when can we get a rack in our lab."

astra-6.text:
Because the unit of deployment for our customers is a rack, not just a chip. You can build a very efficient accelerator, but you still have to make the whole system work—the servers, the networking, the power delivery, the cooling, and the software that ties it all together. If any one of those becomes a bottleneck, the customer doesn’t see the benefit of your silicon.

For inference, that matters because you’re trying to deliver throughput at a particular latency and cost. As you scale across devices and servers, how you move data and coordinate the work becomes critical. So we need rack-scale engineering expertise to turn the chip’s capabilities into a system customers can actually deploy and operate reliably.

sol-6.1.text:
When you deploy into a data center, the customer needs a complete system that fits into their infrastructure. The accelerator is one part of that. You also have to think about how the servers connect, how you deliver power and cooling, and how the software makes all of those resources work together.

For inference, that matters because performance depends on the whole system. You can have a very fast chip and still lose that advantage moving data between devices or waiting on another part of the system. So we see rack-scale engineering as necessary to turn the silicon’s capabilities into something customers can deploy and operate reliably.
